source: Authors not recorded (2026) From Language Models to Control Policies: LLM-driven heuristic synthesis for hot steel rolling
finding: Direct LLM-loop test of restart vs continue. Each LLM search run is treated as a randomized algorithm. A fresh restart gains more than continuing for the first few iterations. The two curves meet near iteration 4.
numbers: 52 independent runs, 730 iterations, Gemini 2.5 Pro, temp 1.0. 50% of runs found their best heuristic by iteration 4 (mean iteration 8). Median best-so-far reward about 30 at iteration 5 and about 40 at iteration 17.
limits: One environment, one LLM. Runs were stopped at different lengths, more often when doing poorly, so per-length distributions come from different subsets. The one-step comparison is myopic.
agent_relevance: Supports a restart trigger early in an attempt, then continuing once past the first few steps. Fits G6 and the S6 trigger.

source: Authors not recorded (2026) From Language Models to Control Policies: LLM-driven heuristic synthesis for hot steel rolling
finding: Whole-allocation comparison: runs of moderate length (10-20 iterations) match the hindsight-optimal split of a fixed budget. One-iteration sampling and very long runs fall behind.
numbers: At T=20 the optimal mix (10+10) is not reliably better than one run of 20 (bootstrap within noise). Runs of 30 iterations underperform at matched budget. Pure 1-iteration sampling is clearly behind as budget grows.
limits: Optimal mix identified in hindsight from the same corpus. Differences between lengths 10 and 20 are inside sampling noise.
agent_relevance: Neither pure best-of-N from scratch nor one endless chain is best. Give each attempt a minimum depth (about 10 steps here) before judging it.

source: Authors not recorded (2026) From Language Models to Control Policies: LLM-driven heuristic synthesis for hot steel rolling
finding: Luby restart schedule run on an LLM search loop. Each sub-run is a fresh conversation reset. It reaches the near-optimal regime without tuning.
numbers: Schedule [5,5,10,5,5,10,20,5,5,10,5,5,10,20,40], 15 sub-runs, 160 iterations. Unseeded campaign: best 51.6, median 34.4. Seeded: best 48.3, median 43.2. Ad-hoc 52 runs: best 55.5, median 30.4, 27 h vs 4.1 h. Simulated Luby (20,000 campaigns) trails the optimum by at most 1.3 reward points up to 160 iterations. Observed campaign at the 39th percentile.
limits: Single unseeded campaign, one seed. The best single heuristic (55.5) came from the ad-hoc runs, not Luby.
agent_relevance: A ready recipe: restart schedule with unit about 5 steps, fresh context each time.

source: Authors not recorded (2026) From Language Models to Control Policies: LLM-driven heuristic synthesis for hot steel rolling
finding: Time-to-threshold test of Luby's guarantee on LLM hit times. Luby with unit 5 stays within a small factor of the best fixed cutoff. Unit 1 is too small and wastes budget.
numbers: Five reward targets. Best fixed cutoff 12 to 24 iterations. Luby u=5 needs 1.1 to 1.8 times the optimum. u=1 costs up to 2.8 times. Luby u=5 beats a fixed 30-iteration restart on 3 of 5 targets and is at most 13% worse on the other 2.
limits: Hit times from the same 52-run corpus, simulated schedule. The unit must be near the natural depth of one attempt.
agent_relevance: Pick the Luby unit as about the number of steps one attempt needs to reach a first local optimum. Too small a unit hurts.

source: Authors not recorded (2026) From Language Models to Control Policies: LLM-driven heuristic synthesis for hot steel rolling
finding: Restarts add depth AND breadth, not breadth alone. Later iterations inside a sub-run usually give the best result. One lucky first iteration sometimes wins.
numbers: In 14 of 15 Luby sub-runs the best reward came from a later iteration (typically 3 to 9), not the first. Sub-run 8 was the exception (first heuristic scored 50.0).
limits: 15 sub-runs only.
agent_relevance: Do not judge an attempt on its first draft. A restart that only samples first drafts is weak.

source: Authors not recorded (2026) From Language Models to Control Policies: LLM-driven heuristic synthesis for hot steel rolling
finding: Pools from many restarts support a portfolio. A small portfolio chosen by simulation beats the single best heuristic, also under cross-validation. Mode collapse inside one run limits diversity; restarts counter it.
numbers: Portfolio of K=4 captures 90% of the oracle gain (60.9 vs oracle 65.1). Held-out half: 61.7 (Luby pool, 156 heuristics) vs 60.6 selected and scored on the same half. The LLM converged on conventional TMCP-style controllers inside a run. Conversation compaction caused amnesia: useful tweaks were rediscovered several times.
limits: Needs a cheap code-run scorer (simulator under 1 s). Domain is steel rolling.
agent_relevance: Portfolio of diverse restarted attempts, chosen by code. Warns that summarised memory loses insights.

source: Zhang et al. (2026) Budget-Aware Anytime Reasoning with LLM-Synthesized Preference Data
finding: Defines the Anytime Index for LLMs: quality of the answer after truncating the chain at each token budget. Tests Grok-3, GPT-oss, GPT-4.1/4o, Llama-3.3 on NaturalPlan trip planning, AIME 2024, GPQA.
numbers: Budget checkpoints 100 to 800 tokens. N=3 traces for evaluation, N=64 for preference data. NaturalPlan trip task has 1,600 instances split into validation and test.
limits: Short budgets (up to 800 tokens on planning). Planning quality measured by constraint satisfaction rate (CSR).
agent_relevance: Gives a measurement for G6: how good is the best-so-far answer when cut off at any time.

source: Zhang et al. (2026) Budget-Aware Anytime Reasoning with LLM-Synthesized Preference Data
finding: Prompting with pairs of good and bad truncated traces from the model itself (PDP) raises anytime quality. The rejected examples add value beyond good examples alone.
numbers: PDP gave a higher Anytime Index than PDP(+) (good examples only) in most of 21 model-dataset settings. Vs LEAP: higher Anytime Index in 6 of 7 models. For strong reasoning models, final accuracy +17.6%, average accuracy +11.4%, Anytime Index +7.9 over LEAP. Llama-3.3-70B NaturalPlan final CSR 82.0 (PDP) vs 76.2 (LEAP).
limits: No fine-tuning. GPT-4.1/4o did not always get the best Anytime Index. Works best when the model can tell good from bad traces.
agent_relevance: In-context contrast examples are cheap and need no training.

source: Zhang et al. (2026) Budget-Aware Anytime Reasoning with LLM-Synthesized Preference Data
finding: Longer reasoning is not always better: GPT-4o on NaturalPlan peaks at a medium budget then declines. Causes named: drift and self-revision of a valid plan, and accumulated small errors.
numbers: GPT-4o CSR peaks mid-budget, then drops slightly by 800 tokens. Smaller GPT-4.1/4o variants still improve past 800 tokens; larger ones plateau.
limits: From appendix text; curve values not tabulated.
agent_relevance: Best-so-far must be stored. The final answer may be worse than an earlier one. Supports G6.

source: Wang et al. (2026) Conformal Thinking: Risk Control for Reasoning on a Compute Budget
finding: Stopping rule with two thresholds: an upper one stops when confident, a lower one stops runs that look unsolvable. Calibrated on a small validation set with distribution-free risk control.
numbers: Validation set of 50 samples (5%), 40 random splits, test 800 samples. Finite-sample correction (UCB) keeps test risk under target; naive cross-validation often crosses the target. The lower threshold saves tokens mainly when unsolvable items are common (1:1 and 1:3 mixes) and adds little at 3:1 solvable.
limits: Models Qwen3-8B, DeepSeek-32B, Qwen-30B, Qwen3-VL-8B; AIME, GPQA, DeepScaleR, MathVision. Exact token savings only in figures.
agent_relevance: A calibrated give-up rule for an attempt (abandon on stalled uncertainty): the restart trigger in anytime form. Still signal-based, consistent with G1.

source: BATS authors (2025) Budget-Aware Tool-Use Enables Effective Agent Scaling
finding: Agents with a larger tool-call budget do not improve unless they see the budget. A budget tracker lets a low budget match a much higher one.
numbers: Gemini-2.5-Pro BrowseComp: ReAct budget 10 = 10.3%, budget 100 = 12.6% (saturates). With Budget Tracker at budget 10 = 12.8%, with 40.4% fewer search calls, 19.9% fewer browse calls, 31.3% lower cost. Mean of 3 runs.
limits: Web-search tasks. Gains are single points.
agent_relevance: Show the agent the remaining budget in plain numbers, as the program already knows it.

source: BATS authors (2025) Budget-Aware Tool-Use Enables Effective Agent Scaling
finding: BATS adds a self-verifier after each attempt that returns SUCCESS, CONTINUE or PIVOT. On PIVOT the trajectory is replaced by a summary of findings and failure causes. This is a restart-with-notes loop inside an LLM agent.
numbers: Gemini-2.5-Pro BrowseComp 12.6 (ReAct) vs 24.6 (BATS); BrowseComp-ZH 31.5 vs 46.0; HLE-Search 20.5 vs 27.0. Claude-Sonnet-4: 12.2 vs 19.1, 29.1 vs 41.5, 20.5 vs 29.0. SLIM baseline 13.4 on BrowseComp. Ablation (early stopping, 2.5-Pro): full 18.7, no planning 17.0, no verification 15.4, neither 14.6.
limits: The verifier is an LLM, so the decision is model-made. That conflicts with our rule that code decides. Constraints are checked by the model, not by a program.
agent_relevance: Pattern to copy: continue vs pivot keyed to remaining budget, with a short failure summary carried across the restart. Make the decision rule code, not model.

source: BATS authors (2025) Budget-Aware Tool-Use Enables Effective Agent Scaling
finding: Budget tracker also helps in other agent domains.
numbers: tau2-bench Retail, Gemini-2.5-Flash, budget 10: Avg@4 47.8% to 55.5%, Pass^4 21.9% to 27.2%. SWE-bench Verified, Gemini-3-Flash-Preview, budget 50: 36.8% to 55.4% resolve rate; tracker at 50 beats baseline at 60 (53.2%).
limits: Appendix results; page text read only to character 100000 of 144432.
agent_relevance: Budget visibility is cheap and transfers across tasks.

source: Brown et al. (2024) Large Language Monkeys: Scaling Inference Compute with Repeated Sampling
finding: Repeated independent sampling is a restart strategy. Coverage (any sample correct) grows nearly log-linearly with number of samples over orders of magnitude, so success time has a long tail that restarts exploit.
numbers: SWE-bench Lite, DeepSeek-Coder-V2-Instruct: 15.9% with 1 sample, 56% with 250 samples, above the single-sample state of the art. Up to 10,000 samples per problem.
limits: Needs a verifier. Gains count only when answers can be checked (code tests).
agent_relevance: Strong case for restarts where a code check exists (G3 held-out check).

source: Brown et al. (2024) Large Language Monkeys: Scaling Inference Compute with Repeated Sampling
finding: Selecting the right sample is the bottleneck. Majority voting and reward models stall while coverage keeps rising.
numbers: MATH, Llama-3-8B-Instruct: coverage 82.9% at 100 samples to 98.44% at 10,000. Majority vote or reward model rose only 40.50% to 41.41% over the same range.
limits: Math word problems; selection quality depends on the verifier.
agent_relevance: Restarts without a real checker do not pay. Matches G4 and G5.

source: Snell et al. (2024) Scaling LLM Test-Time Compute Optimally can be More Effective than Scaling Model Parameters
finding: Sequential revision vs parallel resampling depends on difficulty. Easy questions gain from sequential revision; hard questions needing a different high-level approach gain from independent parallel resampling. A difficulty-adaptive mix wins.
numbers: Compute-optimal revisions beat best-of-N with about 4x less test-time compute (PaLM 2-S*, MATH). Search: beam search beats best-of-N at small budgets; on easy bins beam search over-optimizes the verifier at high budget.
limits: Needs a fine-tuned revision model and a PRM; difficulty from pass@1 bins. One model family.
agent_relevance: Direct evidence for a restart-or-continue switch keyed on difficulty. Difficulty must come from code (pass rate), not model opinion.

source: Chen et al. (2024) Are More LM Calls All You Need? Towards the Scaling Properties of Compound AI Systems
finding: More independent calls can make results worse. Vote accuracy first rises then falls with the number of calls, because easy queries improve and hard queries get worse.
numbers: Non-monotone curves for Vote and Filter-Vote across language tasks. A scaling model predicts the best number of calls from a small sample.
limits: Majority vote of identical-model calls; the drop appears when hard queries have a wrong-answer mode.
agent_relevance: Restarts plus voting is not free: more restarts hurt hard items where the model's wrong answer is the mode. Supports G4.

source: Hassid et al. (2025) Don't Overthink it. Preferring Shorter Thinking Chains for Improved LLM Reasoning
finding: Within one question, the shortest sampled chain is usually more correct than the longest. short-m@k runs k chains in parallel, stops when the first m finish, and votes among them. It is an early-cutoff portfolio, close to a restart policy that kills slow runs.
numbers: Shortest chain up to 34.5% more accurate than longest. short-1@k matches or beats majority voting with up to 40% fewer thinking tokens. short-3@k beats majority voting at all budgets, up to 33% wall-time reduction.
limits: Abstract-level numbers; models and k not read in this session. Reasoning models only.
agent_relevance: Run length is itself a signal: an attempt that goes long is more likely wrong. A length cutoff (kill the slow attempt) is a code-checkable trigger.

source: Wang et al. (2025) Thoughts Are All Over the Place: On the Underthinking of o1-Like LLMs
finding: The opposite failure: models abandon promising lines too early. Wrong answers contain far more thought switches than right ones, and most wrong answers held a correct thought at some point.
numbers: Incorrect responses: about 418% more thought switches and 225% more tokens than correct ones. Over 70% of incorrect responses contain at least one correct thought. Underthinking score (lower is better) e.g. AIME24 QwQ-32B-Preview 65.0, R1-Preview 75.7, R1-671B 37.0.
limits: Open models only (QwQ, R1 family). Switches detected by marker words.
agent_relevance: Restarting too early is as bad as too late. Argues for a minimum depth before any restart, as in the Luby unit result.

source: Wang et al. (2025) Thoughts Are All Over the Place: On the Underthinking of o1-Like LLMs
finding: A decoding penalty on thought-switch tokens (TIP) raises accuracy without training. It suppresses restarts in the wrong places.
numbers: alpha=3, beta=600 chosen on a dev set. AIME2024 pass@1: QwQ-32B-Preview 38.3 to 44.1; R1-Distill-Qwen-32B 61.4 to 64.1; DeepSeek-R1 73.8 to 74.8. GPQA Diamond QwQ 57.6 to 59.1; MATH500-Hard 83.1 to 83.7. Self-consistency with 4 samples: 43.7 to 51.4.
limits: Needs token-logit access. Gains on the easy benchmark are small (0.6).
agent_relevance: An API agent cannot set logits, but a prompt rule 'finish one line before switching' tests the same idea.

source: Huang et al. (2024) Large Language Models Cannot Self-Correct Reasoning Yet
finding: Continuing a chain by self-critique without outside feedback hurts. Fresh resampling does better than self-correction at equal calls.
numbers: GSM8K: GPT-4 95.5 to 91.5 (round 1) to 89.0 (round 2); GPT-3.5 75.9 to 75.1 to 74.7. CommonSenseQA GPT-3.5 75.8 to 38.1 to 41.8. HotpotQA GPT-4 49.0 to 49.0 to 43.0.
limits: Earlier positive claims used oracle stopping or weak first prompts. A 2026 preprint reports weaker models self-correct more often (26.8% vs 16.7%); seen only in a search snippet.
agent_relevance: Continue-with-critique is a worse default than restart unless the revision cites real failing output (G2).

source: Huang et al. (2024) Large Language Models Cannot Self-Correct Reasoning Yet
finding: Equal-call comparison: multi-agent debate is no better than self-consistency, which is a pure restart-and-vote method.
numbers: GSM8K GPT-3.5: standard 76.7; self-consistency with 3 / 6 / 9 responses = 82.5 / 85.3 / 88.2; debate with 6 and 9 responses = 83.2 / 83.0.
limits: One dataset, one model for this comparison.
agent_relevance: Independent restarts beat interacting continuation at equal cost on this task. Votes remain only a hint (G4).

source: Laban et al. (2025) LLMs Get Lost In Multi-Turn Conversation
finding: A conversation that takes a wrong turn does not recover. Splitting a task over turns cuts performance, mostly through unreliability. Restating everything in one fresh prompt keeps performance.
numbers: 15 LLMs, six tasks. Average drop 39% in the abstract (35% in the Fig 1 caption). Single-turn about 90% vs multi-turn about 65%. Aptitude (90th percentile) down 16%; unreliability (90th minus 10th percentile) up 112%. Concat (all info in one turn) = 95.1% of Full. GPT-4o: Full 93.0, Concat 90.9, Sharded 59.1, Recap 76.6, Snowball 65.3. GPT-4o-mini: 86.8, 84.4, 50.4, 66.5, 61.8.
limits: Tasks sharded by design. Recap uses knowledge of the end of the conversation. Only the first 100,000 characters of the page were read.
agent_relevance: Best evidence for restarting from a clean consolidated prompt vs keeping a long thread.

source: Backtracking paper authors (2025) To Backtrack or Not to Backtrack
finding: Sequential backtracking vs parallel sampling at matched tokens is task dependent. Backtracking wins on Sudoku, loses on CountDown, and costs more FLOPs at the same token count.
numbers: CountDown (17M model, 4096 tokens): direct best-of-n beats backtracking. Sudoku (38M): backtracking beats direct but the gap shrinks at larger budget. GRPO on CountDown: backtracking model nearly 70% at 4096 tokens vs DFS 57%; direct model 42.5% pass@1 (82 of 200). 200 test problems per game. MATH-500: backtracking worse at low compute, similar at high; GPQA backtracking better.
limits: Small models trained from scratch on synthetic games, not prompted LLMs. Exact numbers mostly in figures.
agent_relevance: Search depth of the task decides. Deeper trees favour continuing with backtracking; shallow ones favour fresh samples.

source: Wen et al. (2025) ParaThinker: Native Parallel Thinking as a New Paradigm to Scale LLM Test-time Compute
finding: Names tunnel vision: flawed early tokens lock a long chain into a poor path. Several short independent paths merged beat one long path at the same token count.
numbers: AIME 2024 pass@1, 1.5B: 2x16K = 34.8 vs sequential 32K = 28.3; 8x16K = 48.1 vs sequential 128K = 27.4. 7B: 4x16K = 63.3 vs 56.0; 8x16K = 68.8 vs 52.7. Average gain with 8 paths 12.3% (1.5B), 7.5% (7B), about 7.1% extra latency. Beats majority voting by 4.3% (1.5B) and 2.0% (7B). Flawed prefixes of 0 to 1,600 tokens lowered accuracy.
limits: Requires training a special model. The matched-token baseline is a plain long chain, without restarts or budget forcing.
agent_relevance: Evidence that continuing a long chain wastes budget; restart-style breadth wins at long budgets.

source: Muennighoff et al. (2025) s1: Simple test-time scaling
finding: Continuing the same chain with 'Wait' (budget forcing) gives gains that flatten. Appending 'Wait' beat other strings. The paper claims sequential beats parallel voting on its model.
numbers: AIME24: no extrapolation 50.0; 2x Wait 53.3; 2x Alternatively 50.0; 2x Hmm 50.0. s1 with Wait 4x: 56.7 (AIME24), 36.7 (AIME25) vs 50.0 / 26.7 without. Budget forcing control 100%, scaling slope 15, 56.7. Rejection sampling for short length: 655 tries under a 3,500-token cap, 1 try under 16,000. Flattens at about six times; repeated suppression causes loops.
limits: Small tuned model (s1-32B); one benchmark family. Compared to majority voting on a different base model (Qwen2.5-32B-Instruct), so not like for like.
agent_relevance: An anytime lever by force-extending a chain; it has a ceiling. Compare to restart at equal tokens before adopting.

source: Authors not recorded (2025) The Art of Scaling Test-Time Compute for Large Language Models
finding: Large study: no test-time strategy wins everywhere. Short-horizon reasoning models do better with shorter traces; long-horizon models prefer longer ones on hard problems. Beam search scales poorly. Majority voting is the most reliable but costly.
numbers: Over 30 billion tokens, eight open models (7B to 235B), AIME 2024, 2025-I, 2025-II, GPQA Diamond. R1 accuracy on easy problems 0.95 with short traces vs 0.72 with long traces. Beam accuracy falls sharply once beam size is above 2 for short-horizon models. Longest-trace filtering always below majority vote at equal compute. Best strategy rises monotonically with compute.
limits: Open models only. Read through a summary of the HTML page.
agent_relevance: Choose the stopping and restart policy per model type; test it, do not assume.

source: Huang (2007) The Effect of Restarts on the Efficiency of Clause Learning
finding: Older computational system: SAT solver TINISAT with seven restart policies on 22 industrial benchmark families, 251 instances, 2-hour limit. All restart policies beat no restarts; Luby's universal policy was best overall by a small margin.
numbers: Even the worst restart policy finished 2.43 days sooner and solved 37 more instances than no restarts. Luby unit 32 vs geometric: 1.2x faster in aggregate, 2.5x on one family. No policy best on every family.
limits: Luby's optimality proof is for independent Las Vegas runs; clause learning keeps learned clauses, so runs are not independent.
agent_relevance: Carrying learned info across restarts changes the theory. In an LLM loop, seeding restarts with notes does the same (the steel paper's seeded campaign had lower best but higher median).

source: Kautz, Horvitz, Ruan, Gomes, Selman (2002) Dynamic Restart Policies
finding: Restart cutoff can depend on what the solver shows early. Predict run length from features seen in the first window (10 to 1,000 choice points), then kill runs predicted long. Tested against Luby's policy and the best fixed cutoff.
numbers: A window of 10 choice points gave the lowest expected run time. Decision-tree leaves with under 60% short runs were pruned. Compared with Luby's universal policy and the fixed optimal cutoff on quasigroup problems (Satz and CSP).
limits: Needs training data of past runs; benefits specific to those benchmark families. Exact speedups not extracted.
agent_relevance: Classical form of a restart trigger driven by a signal (G1), not a clock: observe an early feature, predict a long run, restart.

source: Lorenz (2017) Runtime Distributions and Criteria for Restarts
finding: Restarts help only for some runtime distributions: heavy-tailed ones (log-normal, Weibull, Pareto types). Scale does not change whether restarts help; location shifts matter only a little. A condition for the optimal restart time is given.
numbers: Analytic results; optimal restart time unaffected by scale and linear in location.
limits: Theory only; no LLM data. Assumes independent runs.
agent_relevance: Before using restarts on an LLM loop, measure its time-to-success distribution. If it is not heavy-tailed or has a high floor, restarts waste budget.

source: Truchet, Richoux, Codognet (2013) Prediction of Parallel Speed-ups for Las Vegas Algorithms
finding: Parallel independent restarts (multi-walk) speedup can be predicted from the sequential runtime distribution. An exponential distribution gives linear speedup; shifted exponential or lognormal gives less.
numbers: Prediction matches actual speedups very well up to 100 cores (per abstract and intro).
limits: Only the abstract and introduction were read. Local-search solvers, not LLMs.
agent_relevance: The same logic gives the gain of N parallel LLM attempts: read it off the single-attempt success-time curve.

source: Luby, Sinclair, Zuckerman (1993) Optimal speedup of Las Vegas algorithms
finding: Universal schedule 1,1,2,1,1,2,4,... is within a log factor of the best fixed cutoff for any unknown distribution, and no universal schedule beats that by more than a constant. Known only from secondary text (steel paper, Huang 2007), not opened directly.
numbers: Factor O(log) over optimum; matches the formula quoted in the steel paper.
limits: Not opened. Lorenz (2017) says the guarantee does not hold in general (search snippet only).
agent_relevance: Basis for the restart schedule above.

source: Qi et al. (2025) Optimizing Anytime Reasoning via Budget Relative Policy Optimization
finding: Trains the model to give a good answer at any cut-off: truncate thinking at budgets sampled from a prior, make the model summarise, reward each. BRPO reduces variance. Beats GRPO at all thinking budgets.
numbers: Abstract only: 'consistently outperforms GRPO across all thinking budgets'. No numbers read.
limits: Training method, not a prompt. No figures extracted.
agent_relevance: Shows models can be trained to be anytime; our scaffold cannot train, so it must store best-so-far in code.

source: Romera-Paredes et al. (2024) FunSearch: mathematical discoveries from program search with LLMs
finding: LLM program search with islands: periodically the worst-scoring islands are wiped and refilled from the best. A restart built into an LLM evolution loop. Seen in search snippets only.
numbers: Exact reset fraction not confirmed in snippets.
limits: Not opened.
agent_relevance: Template for a scheduled restart of the weakest search branch, decided by score.

source: Authors not recorded (2025) The Sequential Edge: Inverse-Entropy Voting Beats Parallel Self-Consistency at Matched Compute
finding: Claims sequential refinement chains with entropy-weighted voting beat parallel majority voting at the same compute. Only an ablation table was seen in a search snippet.
numbers: GPQA-Diamond GPT-OSS-120B at 6 chains: 74.2% entropy vote vs 70.2% majority. AIME-2024 same model at 9 chains: 66.7% vs 60.0%. AIME-2025 GPT-OSS-20B at 9 chains all methods 56.7%.
limits: Snippet only. Conflicts with ParaThinker (parallel wins), so the direction depends on setup.
agent_relevance: A counter-result to restarts: continuation can win when later chains see earlier ones.
